tips.title: Four Ps, and a design mix of three
tips.body: The **marketing mix** is **product, price, promotion, place**. Inside *product* sits the **design mix**: **function, aesthetics, cost**. Questions often use one name when they mean the other, so check which mix is being asked about before you answer.

tips.title: Profit per unit is the gap, not the percentage
tips.body: Cost-plus gives **price = unit cost + (unit cost × mark-up %)**. The **profit per unit is the money**, not the percentage: a 60% mark-up on £5 earns £3, while a 25% mark-up on £24 earns £6. Always subtract to get the profit.

tips.title: Falling sales means an extension strategy
tips.body: A case mentioning **falling sales** is asking about **decline** and wants an **extension strategy**. Flat sales after growth means **maturity**. Naming the phase first, using the evidence in the case, earns a mark before you have recommended anything.

tips.title: For a 12 marker, change one thing and follow it
tips.body: The marks are in **chains applied to this business**. Take one decision, say what it forces in the other three Ps, then judge and name **what would change your answer**. Edexcel marks these in **three** levels: 1 to 4, 5 to 8, 9 to 12.

steps.title: The marketing mix
steps.body:
The **marketing mix** is the set of decisions a business makes about how it sells something. It is usually remembered as the **four Ps**.

- **Product**: what it is, what it does, how it looks.
- **Price**: what it costs the customer.
- **Promotion**: how customers hear about it.
- **Place**: how it reaches them.

The whole of this topic is about making those four decisions well, and then about the point Edexcel cares about most: they are **not independent**. Change one and the others have to change with it.

A business selling a premium watch cannot advertise it with cut-price leaflets and sell it from a market stall. The product, the price, the promotion and the place all have to say the same thing, or customers stop believing any of it.

That idea has a name, and it is worth using: an **integrated** marketing mix, one where the four elements support each other.

visuals.alt: Four boxes for the marketing mix: product, price, promotion and place, with the decision each one covers

check.prompt: Which of these is part of the marketing mix?
check.solution: The four Ps are **product, price, promotion and place**. Profit, productivity and payroll are not part of the mix.

steps.title: Product: the design mix
steps.body:
Every product is a compromise between three things, and Edexcel calls this the **design mix**.

- **Function**: does it work, and does it do what the customer needs?
- **Aesthetics**: how it looks, feels, sounds or smells.
- **Cost**: what it costs the business to make.

The three pull against one another. Better materials improve aesthetics and often function, but raise cost. Cutting cost usually costs you one of the others.

Which one dominates depends on the product and the customer.

- A fire extinguisher is almost entirely **function**. Nobody buys one because it is beautiful.
- A fashion trainer leans heavily on **aesthetics**, though it still has to be comfortable.
- A supermarket's own-brand basics range is built around **cost**, and is honest about it.

An exam question giving you a business and asking which element matters most wants you to **choose one and justify it from the customer**, not to describe all three.

steps.title: The product life cycle
steps.body:
Most products follow the same shape over their lifetime, and the **product life cycle** plots **sales against time** through four phases.

1. **Introduction.** The product is launched. Sales are low, promotion spending is high, and the business may be making a loss on it.
2. **Growth.** Sales rise quickly as the product catches on. Competitors start to notice.
3. **Maturity.** Sales reach their peak and level off. This is usually the most profitable phase, because development costs are paid off and sales are high.
4. **Decline.** Sales fall, often because tastes change or a better product arrives.

Two things to get right.

- The axes are **sales** against **time**. Not profit, and not price.
- **Maturity is where the money is.** Students often assume growth is the best phase because sales are rising fastest, but in growth the business is still spending heavily to build the market.

steps.title: Differentiation
steps.body:
**Differentiation** means making a product or service **stand out from its competitors**.

It matters for a reason worth stating precisely: a business whose product is **the same as everyone else's** can only compete on **price**, and competing on price means lower profit on every sale.

A differentiated product can do three things a copy cannot.

- **Charge a higher price**, because customers cannot get the same thing elsewhere.
- **Build customer loyalty**, so people return rather than shopping around.
- **Survive a new competitor**, because customers want that product, not just any product.

Differentiation can come from any part of the mix: a genuinely different **product**, a distinctive **brand** built through promotion, or being available in a **place** competitors are not.

In an exam, name *how* the business is different and then say *what that lets it do*. "They are different from other shops" earns nothing on its own.

steps.title: Price: the strategies, and the calculation
steps.body:
A **pricing strategy** is the approach a business takes to setting its price. The ones you should be able to name and use are:

- **Cost-plus**: work out what a unit costs to make, then add a fixed percentage as mark-up.
- **Price skimming**: launch high, to earn as much as possible from customers who want it first, then lower the price later.
- **Penetration pricing**: launch low, to get into a market and win customers quickly, then raise the price once established.
- **Competitive pricing**: set the price close to what rivals charge.
- **Psychological pricing**: £9.99 rather than £10, so it feels like nine pounds rather than ten.

Cost-plus is the one that comes with arithmetic:

$$\text{price} = \text{unit cost} + (\text{unit cost} \times \text{mark-up percentage})$$

steps.title: What influences the price
steps.body:
Edexcel names **four influences on pricing strategies**, and a question asking why a price changed usually wants one of them.

- **Technology.** Customers can compare prices instantly online, so a business that overcharges is found out. Technology also cuts costs, which allows lower prices.
- **Competition.** In a market with many similar rivals, a business has little freedom: price too high and customers switch.
- **Market segments.** A business selling to a **premium** segment can charge much more than one selling to a **budget** segment, for a similar product.
- **The product life cycle.** Price often starts high at launch under skimming, or low under penetration, and changes as the product moves through the phases. In decline, price cuts are common.

These are not separate boxes. A question will usually involve two at once: a mature product in a competitive market with easy online price comparison has very little pricing freedom at all.

steps.title: Technology in promotion
steps.body:
Edexcel names three uses of technology in promotion, and expects you to know what each one is *for*.

- **Targeted advertising online.** Adverts are shown to people whose browsing or purchase history suggests they are interested. It is far less wasteful than advertising to everyone, and it can be measured: the business sees who clicked.
- **Viral advertising via social media.** Content is designed to be **shared by customers themselves**, so it spreads at almost no cost. The catch is that the business loses control: it cannot make something go viral, and if the content is disliked it spreads that way instead.
- **E-newsletters.** Emails to customers who have signed up. They are cheap, they go to people who already have some interest, and they can carry offers directly. Too many, and people unsubscribe.

The pattern is worth noticing: technology makes promotion **cheaper and better targeted**, but it also makes it **easier to annoy people** and harder to control what is said about you.

steps.title: Place: retailers and e-tailers
steps.body:
**Place** is how the product reaches the customer. Edexcel names two methods of distribution.

- **Retailers**: physical shops. The customer can see, touch and take the product away immediately, and staff can advise. But shops cost rent, staff and stock, and each one reaches only its local area.
- **E-tailers**, or **e-commerce**: selling online. It reaches a national or worldwide market with far lower fixed costs, it is open at all hours, and it gathers data on what customers look at. But the customer has to wait for delivery, cannot handle the product, and returns cost the business money.

Most businesses now use **both**, which is worth saying in an answer: a shop for customers who want to try before buying, and a website for reach.

The decision follows from the **product**. Something people need to try on, or want today, argues for a shop. Something standard, or too niche to fill a local shop's shelves, argues for online.

steps.title: The integrated marketing mix
steps.body:
This is 2.2.5, and it is where the marks in the long questions are.

**Each element of the mix influences the others.** A decision about one forces decisions about the rest.

- Choose a **premium product** and you need a **high price**, image-based **promotion**, and a **place** that feels exclusive. Sell it cheaply in a discount shop and customers conclude it is not premium after all.
- Choose **penetration pricing** and you need **volume**, which means **wide distribution** and **promotion that reaches many people quickly**.
- Sell only **online** and your **promotion** must be online too, because that is where your customers are and where a click can become a sale.

When the four elements point the same way, the mix is **integrated**, and that is what builds **competitive advantage**: something a business has that rivals find hard to copy. A rival can copy one element, but copying a whole coherent mix is much harder.

And markets are **dynamic**, meaning they change. Technology, competitors and tastes all move, so a mix that worked five years ago may not work now. A business that never revisits its mix loses its advantage slowly and without noticing.

steps.title: Your turn: read the case for its marketing decisions
steps.body:
**Loom & Last** makes hand-finished wool blankets. Each blanket costs **£24.00** to make. The business sells online only, adds a **25%** mark-up, and promotes through an e-newsletter and photographs on social media. Sales grew quickly for three years but have been flat for the last twelve months.

1. Calculate the selling price, and state the profit on each blanket.
2. Identify the phase of the product life cycle the blankets have reached, and justify your answer from the case.
3. Recommend **one** extension strategy, and explain why it suits this business.
4. Explain **one** way the business's decision to sell online only affects its promotion.
5. Evaluate whether Loom & Last should start selling through a high street shop.

Part 5 is the 12-mark question. Argue both ways, apply everything to **this** business, and finish with a judgement that says what it depends on.

steps.title: Going deeper: building a 12-mark 'evaluate' answer
steps.body:
A 12-mark question is marked in **three levels**: **1 to 4**, **5 to 8**, and **9 to 12**. Not four, whatever a textbook written for another board may show. What moves you up is not more points but **developed chains applied to this business**, and a **judgement that says what it depends on**.

A chain has three links. Take *should Loom & Last open a shop?*

1. **Point**: a shop lets customers feel the wool before buying.
2. **Because**: a hand-finished blanket at a premium price is exactly the kind of product people want to touch first, and online photographs cannot convey texture.
3. **So what**: more visitors convert into buyers, and the average order value may rise because they can see the quality justifies the price.

Then do the same **against**: a shop brings rent, staff and stock costs that a £6-per-blanket margin has to cover, so it needs a large number of sales just to break even, and it reaches only one town when the website already reaches the country.

**Then judge, and make it conditional.** "Loom & Last should not open a shop yet. The case for it rests on customers needing to touch the product, but the business's sales are flat rather than falling, so the cheaper extension strategies should be tried first. If those fail and the flat sales turn out to be caused by customers being unwilling to pay a premium price sight unseen, then a single shop in a city with many potential customers would be worth the risk."

Notice what that does: it decides, it gives the reason, and it names **the evidence that would change the answer**. That last move is what separates the top band.

One more thing. Every point above mentions **Loom & Last**, wool, or the £6 margin. An answer that would read the same about any business cannot reach the top level however well argued it is.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The **marketing mix** is **product, price, promotion, place**.
- **Design mix**: **function**, **aesthetics**, **cost**. They pull against each other; choose the dominant one and justify it from the customer.
- **Product life cycle**: **introduction, growth, maturity, decline**, plotting **sales against time**. **Maturity** is usually the most profitable phase.
- **Extension strategies** respond to **decline**: advertise again, cut the price, add value, new packaging, a new market, a new version. Each has a cost.
- **Differentiation** matters because without it a business can only compete on **price**.
- **Pricing strategies**: cost-plus, price skimming, penetration, competitive, psychological.
- **Cost-plus**: price = unit cost + (unit cost × mark-up %). £8.00 with a 50% mark-up gives £12.00, a profit of £4.00 per unit.
- **Profit per unit is the gap, not the percentage.**
- **Influences on pricing**: **technology**, **competition**, **market segments**, **the product life cycle**.
- **Promotion**: advertising, sponsorship, product trials, special offers, branding. Match the method to the **segment**; a luxury brand avoids discounting.
- **Technology in promotion**: targeted advertising online, viral advertising via social media, e-newsletters. Cheaper and better targeted, but harder to control.
- **Place**: **retailers** and **e-tailers**. Shops let customers try; online reaches further for lower fixed costs. Most use both.
- **An integrated mix** is one where the four elements **support each other**, which builds **competitive advantage** in a **dynamic** market.
- A 12-mark answer is marked in **three levels**: 1 to 4, 5 to 8, 9 to 12.

questions.prompt: Loom & Last makes hand-finished wool blankets, selling online only. Each blanket costs £24.00 to make and is sold with a 25% mark-up. Sales grew quickly for three years but have been flat for the last twelve months. Analyse one extension strategy the business could use.
questions.solution: Flat sales after three years of rapid growth suggest the blankets have reached the maturity phase of the product life cycle, and an extension strategy would be used to push sales up again rather than waiting for decline to begin. One suitable strategy would be to add value by launching the blankets in a range of new colours or in a larger size. This suits Loom and Last in particular because the business already has customers who have bought once and know the quality of the hand finishing, and a new colour or size gives those customers a genuine reason to buy a second blanket rather than a reason to look elsewhere. The business also sells online only and already runs an e-newsletter, so it can tell its existing customers about the new range at almost no cost, which matters when the profit on each blanket is only six pounds and a large advertising campaign would take many sales to pay for. The drawback is that developing a new range takes time and money, and some of the sales may simply be customers who would have bought the original blanket anyway, so the extra sales are smaller than they look. On balance it is still the strongest option for this business, because it builds on the quality that made sales grow in the first place rather than cutting the price and eating into a margin that is already thin.

Level 3 (7 to 9): accurate knowledge and terminology throughout, detailed application to the business throughout, detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning, and a valid, well-reasoned conclusion

questions.modelAnswer:
**The phase.** Three years of rapid growth followed by twelve months of flat sales points to **maturity**. An extension strategy here pushes sales up again rather than waiting for decline.

**The strategy: add value.** Launch the blankets in new colours or a larger size.

**Why it suits this business.** Loom & Last already has customers who have bought once and know the quality of the hand finishing, so a new colour or size gives them a reason to buy **again** rather than look elsewhere. Selling **online only** with an existing **e-newsletter** means it can tell those customers at almost no cost — which matters when the profit per blanket is only **£6.00** and a large advertising campaign would take many sales to pay for.

**The drawback.** Developing a range costs time and money, and some sales will be customers who would have bought the original blanket anyway, so the extra sales are smaller than they look.

**Judgement.** Still the strongest option, because it builds on the quality that drove the growth rather than cutting a price whose margin is already thin.

questions.prompt: Loom & Last sells its hand-finished wool blankets online only, at £30.00 each with a profit of £6.00 per blanket. Sales have been flat for twelve months. Evaluate whether Loom & Last should start selling through a high street shop.
questions.solution: There is a real case for opening a shop. A hand-finished wool blanket at thirty pounds is a product people want to touch before buying, because the appeal is the texture and the quality of the finishing, and a photograph on a website cannot convey either. A shop would let customers feel the wool, which should convert more browsers into buyers and may explain why sales have gone flat, if potential customers are unwilling to pay a premium price for something they cannot examine. A shop would also add a new element to the marketing mix that reinforces the premium positioning, since a well presented shop says the same thing about quality that the product itself is saying. Against that, a shop brings rent, staff wages and stock costs, all of which are fixed and have to be paid whether blankets sell or not. With a profit of only six pounds on each blanket, the business would need to sell a very large number of blankets every month simply to cover those costs before making any extra profit at all. A single shop also reaches only one town, whereas the website already reaches the whole country, so the business would be spending heavily to serve a much smaller market. There are cheaper ways to address the same problem, such as offering free returns or sending fabric samples, which would let customers judge the texture without any fixed costs. On balance Loom and Last should not open a shop yet. The strongest argument for one is that customers need to touch the product, but that argument can be tested far more cheaply first. If sending samples and offering free returns lifted sales substantially, that would confirm touch is the barrier and would make a single shop in a large city worth the risk, and if it did not, the flat sales are being caused by something else and a shop would not have fixed it either.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 4): some knowledge with little business terminology, limited application to the business, few connections between points, and a conclusion resting on generic assertions

Level 2 (5 to 8): mostly accurate knowledge with terminology in places, sound application to the business though not always consistent, chains of reasoning that connect points, and a conclusion based on sound evaluation

Level 3 (9 to 12): accurate knowledge and terminology throughout, detailed application to the business throughout, detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning, and a valid, well-reasoned conclusion

criteria.text: Argues for the shop with a chain applied to this product, such as customers needing to feel the wool
Argues against with a chain using the fixed costs against the £6 margin, or the limited reach of one town
Reaches a supported judgement that names what it depends on, or the cheaper test that would settle it

questions.modelAnswer:
**For.** A hand-finished wool blanket sells on **texture and quality of finish**, neither of which a photograph conveys. A shop lets customers **feel the wool**, which should convert more browsers into buyers — and may be exactly why sales have gone flat, if people will not pay £30.00 for something they cannot examine. A well-presented shop also **reinforces the premium positioning**, so the place element agrees with the product.

**Against.** Rent, wages and stock are **fixed costs**, payable whether blankets sell or not. On a profit of **£6.00 per blanket**, the business must sell a very large number every month just to cover them. And one shop reaches **one town**, where the website already reaches the country — heavy spending to serve a smaller market.

**The cheaper test.** Free returns, or sending **fabric samples**, would let customers judge the texture with **no fixed costs**.

**Judgement.** Not yet. The strongest argument for a shop is that customers need to touch the product — and that can be tested far more cheaply first. **If** samples and free returns lift sales substantially, touch is confirmed as the barrier and one shop in a large city becomes worth the risk. **If they do not**, something else is causing the flat sales and a shop would not have fixed it either.

Notice the judgement names **the evidence that would change the answer**. That is what reaches Level 3.

examTechnique.body:
Read the case before the question, and underline the numbers: a unit cost, a mark-up, a trend in sales. They are there to be used.

For a calculation, show the mark-up as its own line before adding it to the cost, and make sure you answer what was asked: the **price** and the **profit per unit** are different numbers.

For a life cycle question, name the phase **and quote the evidence from the case** that puts it there. Flat sales after growth is maturity; falling sales is decline.

For a recommendation, choose **one** option and argue it. Listing three unranked options scores less than one developed choice.

For any 9 or 12 mark question, build **chains**: point, because, so what. Then judge, and say **what your judgement depends on** or what evidence would change it.

Apply everything to the named business. An answer that would read identically about any company cannot reach the top level, however fluent it is.
examinerErrors: Confusing the marketing mix with the design mix. The design mix is function, aesthetics and cost.
Giving the mark-up percentage when the question asked for the profit per unit in pounds.
Saying growth is the most profitable phase. Maturity is, because launch costs have been recovered.
Recommending an extension strategy without naming the life cycle phase or the evidence for it.
Listing several options instead of choosing one and developing it.
Writing about the marketing mix in general without applying anything to the business in the case.
Reaching no judgement at all on an *evaluate* question, or a judgement with no reason.
Treating the four Ps as independent, when a change in one forces changes in the others.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer treats the mix as a system rather than a list, so a change in one element is followed through into the other three without being asked. It names the life cycle phase from the evidence in the case rather than asserting it. It uses the numbers it is given, and it knows the difference between a mark-up percentage and the money earned on a unit, which it brings into the argument when weighing a fixed cost. It develops two or three chains fully instead of mentioning six things, argues both ways, and ends with a judgement that names the circumstances or the evidence that would change it. Every sentence could only have been written about the business in front of it.
